sections.text: Introduction High research interest in the development of sustainable and efficient technology for energy storage is induced by a ubiquitous demand for energy and the established environmental crisis by the prevailing use of fossil fuels [ 1 ]. Hydrogen is of paramount interest as an alternative to conventional fossil fuels owing to its high energy density and carbon-free combustion products [ 2 ]. The hydrogen storage is one of the unwelcome issues in the development of hydrogen energy. Although hydrogen is an energy-intensive and environmentally benign energy carrier that holds great promise to meet long-term storage targets, the application of hydrogen will become stagnant unless impediments like its production, storage, and transportation are resolved [ 3 ]. Hydrogen storage conditions determine the energy cost of a method: the higher the hydrogen pressure and the difference between the storage temperature and the ambient temperature, the higher the energy cost. The optimal method should combine high hydrogen storage density with low energy consumption [ 4 ]. To pave the way to a practically viable hydrogen storage system, the low total mass of the storage system is essential [ 5 ,  6 ]. The underlying target of developing hydrogen storage materials is to enable their safe distribution to other sectors while also stronging usage as onboard fuel cell cars at ambient temperature. There are technical targets for onboard hydrogen storage systems set by three organizations, namely, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) (DOE, 2022), the Fuel Cells and Hydrogen Joint Undertaking (FCH JU) in Europe, and the New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization (NEDO) (NEDO, 2015) in Japan. Based on these targets, the gravimetric density of hydrogen and cost should be around 6.5 wt% and 266 USD/kg (Table  1 ). Currently, no materials can meet the requirements. Table 1 Comparison of DOE targets in the US, FCH JU in Europe, and NEDO in Japan Targets Gravimetric density kWh/kg system (kg H 2 /kg) Volumetric density kWh/L system (kg H 2 /L system) Storage system cost $/kWh ($/kg H 2 ) DOE 2.2 (0.065) 1.7 (0.050) $8 ($266) FCH JU 1.2 (0.035) 2 (0.060) $10.40 ($338) NEDO 2.5 (0.075) 2.36 (0.071) $5.4 ($180) Creating a storage technology that is competitive, compact, and ecologically sustainable will enhance the ability of hydrogen to rival natural and synthetic fuels in the market effectively. At present, the most widely utilized and commercially available hydrogen storage technologies are compressed gas and liquid storage. However, there is a rapidly growing interest in emerging solid-state hydrogen storage materials as alternative solutions. Hydrogen can be implemented into porous materials or metal hydrides via chemisorption and physicochemical or physisorption interactions [ 7 ]. While chemisorption interaction, which mainly occurs in metal hydrides, is based on a vigorous reaction with hydrogen molecules [ 7 ], physisorption (porous materials such as zeolites, MOFs, activated carbon, and other carbon-based materials) occurs through weak and long-range interactions. Thus, physical–chemical interaction is considered the most pertinent for the development of solid hydrogen storage materials because, according to DOE [ 7 ], it requires an appropriate range of temperature (− 40 to 85 °C) and pressure (< 100 atm) for on-board purposes. Carbon materials are highly promising for hydrogen storage due to their high stability, low cost, and scalability. However, their reliance on physisorption limits their hydrogen storage capacity at ambient conditions compared to chemisorption-based materials like metal and complex hydrides. Among the porous materials extensively studied, MOFs and COFs stand out due to their tunable structures, high crystallinity, and consistent synthesis processes [ 8 ]. Their exceptionally high surface area makes them particularly appealing for hydrogen storage applications. Additionally, MOFs offer unique merits through the presence of metal binding sites and the ability to post-synthetically modify linkers, setting them apart from other porous materials. However, a significant drawback of MOFs, COFs, and porous polymers like PIMs lies in their limitations. Despite their high surface area, these materials often suffer from relatively poor chemical and thermal stability, as well as obstacles in achieving sustainable large-scale synthesis [ 8 ]. In contrast, porous carbon presents a cost-effective alternative. It can be synthesized more easily on an industrial scale and derived from recyclable, carbon-rich waste materials, comprising bio-based precursors. Recently, porous carbons have garnered significant attention due to their numerous advantages over other materials. Their superior chemical and thermal stability compared to MOFs and porous polymers, along with a wide range of optimization strategies to enhance hydrogen storage capacity, make them a promising choice for practical applications. Due to their unique geometry, super conductivity, and adjustable micro-structure, functional carbon materials have been extensively introduced into hydrogen storage systems as host materials, barrier layers, and catalyzers. In addition, considerable attention has been given to carbon-based materials owing to their low cost, low weight, high surface area, high chemical stability, morphologies variations, and specific interaction between gas molecules and carbon atoms as potential hydrogen storage materials [ 9 ]. Carbon-based materials can densely pack the hydrogen gas molecules with protection and persistence. Figure  1  reveals their advantages and disadvantages. Fig. 1 Scheme of pros and cons of carbon materials applied for hydrogen storage systems It is well known that a hydrogen molecule forms a link with a typical carbon-based arrangement by mild van der Waals interactions, with an energy range of 0.04 to 0.12 eV [ 10 ]. In this case, most carbon atoms are in sp 2  hybridization. In contrast, when a hydrogen atom reacts chemically with a carbon atom, orbital hybridization shifts from sp 2  to sp 3 , producing a binding energy between 2 and 3 eV Fig.  2 . Fig. 2 The hybridization of carbon in the graphene sheet Moreover, a computational study has shown that graphene or carbon nanotubes have the potential to be used as hydrogen storage materials [ 11 ]. Earlier studies reported that the higher electron affinity of carbon nanoparticles depends on the structure of carbon-based materials. As demonstrated in Fig.  3 , a higher number of pores, folding, and angles, and higher electron affinity make the Desorption of hydrogen easier [ 12 ]. Fig. 3 Correlation of electron affinity and hydrogen removal energy (adopted from [ 12 ]) Carbon atoms can form covalent bonds with three, five, or seven adjacent carbon atoms, potentially creating pentagonal and heptagonal surfaces. These surface configurations facilitate the presence of intricate solids and large molecules like activated carbon, graphite, diamond, carbon nanofibers, fullerene structures, single-wall nanotubes, and multi-wall nanotubes. Cutting-edge science and engineering are enabling the synthesis of a range of nanostructured carbon materials, comprising zero-dimensional (NPs, fullerenes, quantum dots) [ 13 – 15 ], 1-dimensional (carbon nanotubes (single-walled carbon nanotubes, multiwalled carbon nanotubes), carbon nanofibers) [ 16 – 18 ], 2-dimensional (graphene sheets) [ 19 – 22 ] and 3-dimensional (carbon nano-onions, carbon nanospheres, mesoporous carbon) [ 23 – 25 ] structures etc. have aroused great interest in the research community due to their unique structural properties as shown in Fig.  4 . In Fig.  5 , the steps in carbon materials modification implemented in hydrogen storage systems ranging from the twentieth century up to present days are described [ 26 – 30 ]. Currently, novel hybrid structures are based on a combination of materials with distinct morphologies and dimensions [ 31 ]. Fig. 4 Schematic for the molecular models of carbon nanostructures Fig. 5 Scheme of the early development of carbon-based materials for hydrogen storage systems This review highlights the carbon materials with different morphological structure dimensionalities from 0 to 3D that are under investigation, encompassing the synthesis procedures and their structure-related hydrogen storage performances when applied as hydrogen storage material. This is followed by a discussion of current approaches and strategies for enhancing hydrogen storage properties using carbon-derived substances. The features of 0D, 1D, 2D, and 3D carbonaceous materials are also mentioned with examples. This review aims to accentuate the critical importance of dimensionality and morphological structure, thus investigating their influence on carbon materials design applied in hydrogen storage systems.

Techniques for developing carbon materials Physisorption of hydrogen Adsorption occurs when molecules of gases and vapors are attracted to solid surfaces. Physical adsorption of gas molecules on the surface of a solid results from resonance fluctuations in the charge distribution. Physisorption involves a gas molecule interacting with multiple atoms on a solid surface. Physisorption can also be called dispersion compounding with short-range repulsive contact between phases, referred to as van der Waals interaction. Another argument made by Panella et al. [ 32 ] is that forces with the long-range act on the molecules, changing their charge distribution. This, in turn, causes increased induced dipoles and starts the interaction. Still, as the electron clouds from close neighbors are interpenetrated, nearby gas particles are more repelled by one another. In the gas–solid system, the Lennard–Jones potential may be applied to show the interaction between the adsorbent and the gas molecules. Figure  6  shows the energy vs. distance scale from the adsorbent surface regarding the potential energy of chemisorbed and physisorbed hydrogen. The term ‘physical adsorption’ implies that there is no energy barrier to ‘lock’ gas molecules out from such a surface, as depicted below in Fig.  6 . As such, there is no activation step, and physical adsorption is fast kinetically except for diffusional limitation. Heterogeneous physisorption of molecular hydrogen is estimated to vary in a range from 1 to 10 kJ mol–1, which is ten times smaller than the values characteristic of chemisorption processes [ 33 ]. Fig. 6 A correlation of the potential energy of chemisorbed and physisorbed hydrogen to the distance from the surface Due to the weak interaction of carbonaceous materials with hydrogen, substantial physisorption is only observed at low temperatures (< 273 K) and is unsuitable for application in ambient conditions. The two mechanisms by which hydrogen is adsorbed on carbon nanomaterials are (i) the Kubas interaction and (ii) the spillover mechanism, both of which are well discussed by Nagar et al. [ 34 ]. The Kubas interaction mechanism involves the transfer of a charge from the highest occupied orbital of the H 2  ligand to the vacant metal d-orbitals, followed by a transfer back to the lowest unoccupied orbital of the ligand. Another mechanism known as spillover is described as the dissociation of hydrogen molecules into hydrogen atoms that are physisorbed to nanoparticles of metals. It is well known that they polarize when hydrogen molecules approach metal nanoparticles. The H–H bond starts to relieve, and thus, the hydrogen atoms can chemisorb on the particles. Consequently, the hydrogen atoms migrate and distribute over the adsorbate, commonly the supporting material of the metal nanoparticle, as the latter becomes saturated. The hydrogen atoms must be moved across the adsorbate from one metal nanoparticle-supporting adsorbate material to another. This can be quickly done if the contact between the adsorbate material and the metal nanoparticles is not a barrier to the hydrogen atom movement and is pivotal for the so-called ‘spilling’ of the hydrogen atoms across the adsorbate surface [ 34 ]. Different factors, namely surface area and pore structure, may also affect the hydrogen sorption mechanism in carbon-based materials. According to Li et al., the adsorption mechanism involves (1) hydrogen interacting with the material surface and (2) hydrogen molecules permeating between the layers of carbon atoms [ 35 ]. Moreover, it has been reported that the number of pores with the sub-nanometer size is considerably dominant if speaking about hydrogen storage through physisorption on porous carbon materials [ 36 ]. There is a statement that pores between 1.5 and 0.5 nm enhance the storage of hydrogen because they help to strengthen the energy of interaction between hydrogen molecules and carbon material pore walls [ 36 ]. Nagar et al. revealed that an increase in the distance between different graphene layers can improve the free energy of physisorption and the binding energy of H 2  on graphene surfaces. 6–7 Å interlayer spacing was found to provide the highest volumetric density [ 34 ]. Physical activation of carbon materials for hydrogen storage Commercial physical activation is a two-stage operation consisting of pyrolysis in a neutral atmosphere followed by activation in oxidizing atmospheric gases such as steam, carbon dioxide, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen or air mixtures at elevated temperatures in the interval of 800–1100 °C [ 37 ]. With this technique, it is possible to acquire activated carbon with a porous structure and excellent physical performance, which is considered a clean solution due to the absence of chemical agents [ 38 ]. In the process of physical activation of activated carbon, the prolonged activation time, the poor low adsorption capacity of the treated activated carbon, as well as excessive energy consumption are the major drawbacks [ 39 ]. While physical activation has the advantage of not requiring corrosive and costly chemical as activators, resulting in lower production costs and a more environmentally friendly and simple operation, it presents challenges in accurately tuning the activation process and results in a relatively disordered porous structure [ 40 ]. The authors investigated the surface and pore structure properties and the hydrogen storage performance at ambient temperature of the super-activated carbon (SAC) materials fabricated by CO 2  activation of template porous carbons [ 41 ]. Activation is performed by placing the prepared carbon materials in the center of the quartz tube in the tube furnace, heating it to the activation temperature (1223 K) under nitrogen (5 K/min), followed by switching the gas flow to CO 2  (30 cm 3 /min). After cooling to room temperature under nitrogen, the SAC sample was obtained after activation with CO 2 . SAC materials were found to possess high specific surface areas of up to 2829 m 2 /g and large pore volumes of up to 2.34 cm 3 /g, much higher than unactivated materials. In this [ 42 ], ACS samples were prepared from amorphous cellulose and characterized in texture and hydrogen adsorption. Samples were obtained by applying a physical activation pyrolysis method with two different pre-treatment steps, namely “cutting” (APAC) and “reducing in flakes” (AFPAC) methods, respectively. The activation reached 900 °C under constant CO 2  flow. Most activated pores are smaller than 1 nm in diameter, with the mean value ranging from 0.5 to 0.6 nm, which is the ultra-microporous range. The reported structure has a strong influence on the H 2  adsorption properties. At 1 bar and − 196 °C, it reaches values very close to the ideal monolayer coverage where H 2  molecules form a single layer with the liquid H 2  density on the surface. Chemical activation of carbon materials Chemical activation is a highly effective strategy for enhancing the hydrogen sorption properties of carbon materials derived from coal or biomass. This approach employs a single-step pyrolysis process conducted in the presence of a chemical activating agent. A range of chemical agents has been utilized for this purpose, including phosphoric acid, zinc chloride, and alkaline hydroxides such as KOH. It has been noted that alkaline hydroxides, particularly KOH, can yield materials with improved surface areas and pore volumes. High surface areas (> 2000 m 2 /g), large pore volume (about 1 cm 3 /g), and uniform distribution of micropore sizes in the range of 1–2 nm and small mesopores are particularly characteristic of activated carbons produced with KOH as the activating agent. The carbon structure is oxidized to generate carbonate ions and pores. Chemical activation offers multiple benefits, containing a reduced processing temperature, shorter reaction duration, and enhanced prevalence of micropores. However, it is hampered by the need to eliminate impurities produced during the activation procedure effectively. In the study conducted by [ 43 ] the wood samples were activated with KOH and phosphoric acid. They revealed that activated carbon has remarkably elevated levels of hydrogen absorption under nearly room temperature conditions and moderate pressures (up to 0.8 wt% at 25 °C and 20 bar). It is also noted that the adsorption's heat at zero coverage and the change in enthalpy throughout the gradual process showed substantial uptake levels, 10.9 kJ/mol and 17–20 kJ/mol, respectively. These results were unusual and exceeded the typical values reported for carbon-based materials previously [ 43 ]. The hydrothermal carbonization followed by alkaline activation methods was used by Sangchoom et al. [ 44 ] and activated carbons (ACs) showed notable hydrogen absorption capacity, ranging from 3.6 to 6.2% at a pressure of 20 bar with a surface area of 3235 m 2 /g. In a recent study, activated carbon derived from biomass (Palimera sprout) with KOH activation accomplished a hydrogen uptake of approximately 1.06 wt% under conditions of room temperature and 15 bar [ 45 ]. Chemical activation is also applied to develop porosity in carbon nanofibers. Authors found that with only a specific surface area ranging from 1500 to 1700 m 2 /g, it was possible to achieve a total hydrogen storage capacity of approximately 34 g H 2  per liter at a temperature of 77 K and pressure of 40 bar [ 46 ]. Most of the studies showed a positive effect of chemical activation on hydrogen storage capacity [ 47 – 49 ]. Application of the method allows biomass waste, food waste, and other carbon precursors to be utilized as hydrogen storage material. Incorporation of elements or dopants/defects Previous research showed that elements or dopants could be implemented to enrich reaction speed at mild conditions and achieve appropriate hydrogen sorption characteristics. Catalysts with high surface area contribute to altered surface interactions, dissociation of hydrogen molecules, and advanced sorption/desorption parameters. The doping of catalysts is one of the most essential routes in enhancing the hydrogen adsorption/desorption kinetics of hydrogen storage devices. By inducing the rapid separation/bonding of hydrogen molecules/atoms, the critical role is to lift the hydrogen storage performance of the material. Catalyst doping of the carbon host can be seen in Fig.  7 , which enhances hydrogen-carbon bond energy. Carbon nanomaterials can be altered by incorporating elements such as free metals, metal oxides, and alloys to enhance hydrogen storage capacity. 3d transition metals (Ni, Nb, Pd, etc.) catalysis facilitates the hydrogenation process by improving the dissociation rate of hydrogen molecules [ 50 ]. The formation of the Mg 2 Ni phase at the interface between the MgH 2  phase and the Ni catalyst after hydrogenation is the primary reason for the superior hydrogen desorption properties of Ni-doped MgH 2 . A further explanation is that activation energy for hydrogen desorption is reduced when Ni is added. The dissociation rate of hydrogen is based on the metal catalyst's high surface area to volume ratio. Specific emphasis is received by carbon additives, entailing nanotubes, carbon black, graphite, etc. [ 51 – 55 ]. Furthermore, nanoparticles' larger surface and porosity furnish additional area and pore binding sites to enhance storage density. Hence, porous nanostructured materials can generally enhance gravimetric and volumetric storage densities. The following sections will examine the latest research on carbon materials, divided according to their dimensions and structures. They will also review synthesis routes, the pros and cons of nanomaterials, their potential to preserve hydrogen, and feasible enhancement approaches. This review is expected to contribute to the existing knowledge in this field.

Nanostructuring and nanoconfinement of metal hydrides with carbon materials Another way to overcome the kinetic barriers associated with diffusion is to move to nanostructured/nanoscale materials. The surface atoms in nanosized materials have high surface energy and can easily combine with other atoms to transform into stable states. However, nanoscale materials are susceptible to accumulation and even sintering at elevated temperatures. For some hydrides, the synthesis of nanoparticles is very complicated in principle. By classifying the nanoparticles within the support material or so-called nanoconfinement, as shown in Fig.  8 , the utilization of nanostructured supports is a viable way to impede particle growth and accumulation of the hydride, which also maintains the dehydrated products in close contact by restricting their mobility. In addition, the supporting material should be chemically inert, stable under the conditions necessary for hydrogen release and uptake, and sufficiently light to retain a high gravimetric hydrogen storage capacity for the nanocomposite. Furthermore, a support material with catalytic activity can facilitate hydrogen's chemical desorption and absorption. Significant growth has been made in using nanomaterials as structural and catalytic supports to advance the hydrogen storage performance of various hydrides. Fig. 8 Schematic representation of hydrogen storage in nanomaterials via molecular storage ( a–c ) or nanoconfinement ( d ) (modified from [ 70 ,  71 ]) Multiple techniques for fabricating materials under nanoconfinement conditions, i.e., with size restrictions owing to the confined nanoscale volume, have been evolved to resolve these issues. Nanoconfinement was first used to enhance the kinetics of NaAlH 4  by placing the hydride in carbon aerogels [ 72 ]. Microporous activated carbon, graphene, polymeric and carbon nanotubes, hollow carbon nanospheres, metal–organic framework materials, etc., have also been used as limiting frameworks [ 73 ]. Using theoretical and experimental methods, the authors reported Li 3 N[LiNH 2  + 2LiH] under nanoconfinement conditions in nanoporous carbon with pore size ~ 3 nm. They showed that the presence of nanosurfaces radically changes the hydrogen absorption and release processes. The formation of an undesirable intermediate phase (Li 2 NH) is suppressed, and the kinetics and reversibility are dramatically improved. A further finding shows the catalytic action of Co@C nanoflowers, which enriches the sorption/desorption of MgH 2  [ 74 ]. The addition of carbon nanotubes contributes to improved kinetics for both simple metal hydrides (e.g., MgH 2 ) and complex hydrides (NaAlH 4 , Li-Mg-N–H, LiBH 4 , Li-Mg-B-H) [ 75 ,  76 ]. This is due to their unique structure, which creates diffusion channels for hydrogen, the presence of impurity metal nanoparticles, and electronic characteristics. For Mg hydrides modified with various carbon-based materials, it was found that that multi-layered surface folds are beneficial in maintaining the high dispersibility and nano-size of Mg/MgH 2  NPs, thereby improving the thermodynamic and kinetic properties of the hydrogen storage system [ 77 ]. Thus, multi-layered carbon materials such as graphite, multi-layered graphene, MWCNTs, carbon nanofibers (e.g., bamboo-shaped carbon nanotubes), and porous carbons are highly attractive for hydrogen storage.

One-dimensional carbon materials One-dimensional (1D) materials have been the subject of much development and have had applications in many areas through their unique large surface linear morphology, easy relief of tension when cycling, and an efficient electron transport pathway to accomplish superb electrochemical performance [ 83 ]. 1D nanostructures typically range in diameter from 1 to 100 nm and possess a high aspect ratio [ 84 ]. The morphology can be filamentary, tubular, rod-shaped, fibrous, or ribbon-shaped. Hydrothermal route, vapor deposition method, sol–gel method, template method, and electrospinning method are the main techniques for acquiring 1D nanostructures. Therefore, based on the characteristics of 1D nanomaterials (NMs), it has significant advantages in light capture, electron and ion transmission, and mass loading and diffusion and has a vital application prospect in the field of mesoscopic, energy storage and conversion [ 85 ,  86 ], nano-optoelectronic devices [ 87 ], photocatalysis [ 88 ], and electrocatalysis [ 89 ]. 1D NMs have received exceptional consideration as potential storage materials given their low cost, easy accessibility, good recycling characteristics, low densities, vast diversities of bulk and pore structures, and reasonably good chemical stability. For example, carbon nanotubes (CNTs) are one-dimensional materials with a hollow geometry that exhibit a significant specific surface area, superior electrical conductivity, and outstanding mechanical strength and thermal conductivity. Multi-wall carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) are metallic, whereas single-wall carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) are semiconducting, dependent on their helicity and diameter, and can significantly influence charge transfer processes. As appealing supports for heterogeneous catalysts, CNTs are considered ideal and unique templates for immobilizing/depositing metallic nanoparticles (NPs) to build nanostructures. Hydrogen might be stored in a bunch of carbon nanotubes, with H 2  molecules physisorbed on the outer surfaces of the CNTs or interstitial areas among the CNTs, which separate the distances between the tubes in a pressurized environment. Previous studies of hydrogen storage in carbon nanotubes contended high storage capacities and were the impetus for extensive research worldwide. Further investigation revealed that the hydrogen adsorptive capacity was primarily a function of the specific surface area of the carbonaceous material [ 90 – 93 ]. Various studies have shown that physisorbed and chemisorbed hydrogen species can be stored in CNTs at gravimetric densities of 0.1–6.3 wt% and pressures of 0.01–20 MPa [ 94 – 96 ]. Although CNTs appear to be more efficient at storing hydrogen than metal hydrides, the storage pressure in CNTs is approximately 5–10 times higher, resulting in increased storage costs. One-dimensional carbon materials One-dimensional (1D) materials have been the subject of much development and have had applications in many areas through their unique large surface linear morphology, easy relief of tension when cycling, and an efficient electron transport pathway to accomplish superb electrochemical performance [ 83 ]. 1D nanostructures typically range in diameter from 1 to 100 nm and possess a high aspect ratio [ 84 ]. The morphology can be filamentary, tubular, rod-shaped, fibrous, or ribbon-shaped. Hydrothermal route, vapor deposition method, sol–gel method, template method, and electrospinning method are the main techniques for acquiring 1D nanostructures. Therefore, based on the characteristics of 1D nanomaterials (NMs), it has significant advantages in light capture, electron and ion transmission, and mass loading and diffusion and has a vital application prospect in the field of mesoscopic, energy storage and conversion [ 85 ,  86 ], nano-optoelectronic devices [ 87 ], photocatalysis [ 88 ], and electrocatalysis [ 89 ]. 1D NMs have received exceptional consideration as potential storage materials given their low cost, easy accessibility, good recycling characteristics, low densities, vast diversities of bulk and pore structures, and reasonably good chemical stability. For example, carbon nanotubes (CNTs) are one-dimensional materials with a hollow geometry that exhibit a significant specific surface area, superior electrical conductivity, and outstanding mechanical strength and thermal conductivity. Multi-wall carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) are metallic, whereas single-wall carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) are semiconducting, dependent on their helicity and diameter, and can significantly influence charge transfer processes. As appealing supports for heterogeneous catalysts, CNTs are considered ideal and unique templates for immobilizing/depositing metallic nanoparticles (NPs) to build nanostructures. Hydrogen might be stored in a bunch of carbon nanotubes, with H 2  molecules physisorbed on the outer surfaces of the CNTs or interstitial areas among the CNTs, which separate the distances between the tubes in a pressurized environment. Previous studies of hydrogen storage in carbon nanotubes contended high storage capacities and were the impetus for extensive research worldwide. Further investigation revealed that the hydrogen adsorptive capacity was primarily a function of the specific surface area of the carbonaceous material [ 90 – 93 ]. Various studies have shown that physisorbed and chemisorbed hydrogen species can be stored in CNTs at gravimetric densities of 0.1–6.3 wt% and pressures of 0.01–20 MPa [ 94 – 96 ]. Although CNTs appear to be more efficient at storing hydrogen than metal hydrides, the storage pressure in CNTs is approximately 5–10 times higher, resulting in increased storage costs. Following the surfactant model, the “magnesophilic end” of the NiFe combines with the Mg/MgH 2  to form Mg 2 Ni/Mg 2 NiH 4  and α-Fe, while the “magnesiphobic end” of the CNT is broken down into a dispersion medium upon mechanical ball milling and hydrogen combustion. Hydrogen storage mechanisms of these materials is based on physisorption and spillover effect, where high surface area and curvature enable moderate hydrogen adsorption and they can act as a bridge for hydrogen spillover from a catalyst. Pristine CNTs have a tendency to aggregate due to van der Waals forces. The material offers significant advantages, including high volumetric and gravimetric hydrogen storage capacities, extensive tunability of pore size and distribution, and scalable, cost-efficient production techniques, such as those utilizing biomass. The drawbacks associated with 3D materials encompass lower electronic conductivity compared to their 2D counterparts, and the critical need for pore size optimization to enrich adsorption performance. Carbon aerogels provide hierarchical porosity and outstanding cryogenic storage potential, whereas porous carbon materials are both cost-effective and easily scalable. Future research will likely focus on optimizing their properties through functionalization and hybridization with other materials to achieve practical hydrogen storage systems.

Summary and outlook This review summarizes the various routes for the design and synthesis of carbon nanomaterials that have been developed and studied extensively for their application in the field of hydrogen storage. Research on carbon nanomaterials has continually attracted significant attention and has resulted in pivotal advances. They are highly sought-after in a variety of fields, including lithium-ion battery materials, optoelectronic materials, catalyst carriers, chemical and biological sensors, hydrogen storage materials, supercapacitor materials, and other significant applications due to their distinctive structure and exceptional physical and chemical properties. Generally, carbon materials ranging from 0D to 3D are considered promising hydrogen storage materials owing to their chemical stability, low molar mass, high surface area, and variations of different forms and structures. The surface area of carbonaceous materials is regarded as one of the pivotal aspects of hydrogen sorption properties since hydrogen storage capacity is proportional to a given area. Taking this into consideration, efficient hydrogen storage via carbon-based materials is established on porous spatial structures along with high surface area. Thus, structural and spatial alterations or catalytic enhancements of carbon-based materials are necessary for building safe, reliable, and high-surface-area hydrogen storage systems working at moderate conditions. The activity of carbon materials for hydrogen storage varies significantly depending on their dimensional structure. These discrepancies arise due to variations in surface area, pore structure, electronic properties, and interaction mechanisms with hydrogen. For most practical hydrogen storage applications, 3D carbon materials are the best option due to their balance of high storage capacity, scalability, and cost-effectiveness. They are particularly effective for physisorption-based storage at cryogenic temperatures. At room temperature, weak hydrogen-carbon interactions hinder effective hydrogen retention, but at 77 K, reduced molecular kinetic energy allows efficient physisorption on the large surface area and microporous structure of 3D materials. For cutting-edge, high-efficiency designs that incorporate room-temperature storage, 2D carbon materials offer a promising path forward, provided the challenges of aggregation and cost can be addressed. For room-temperature storage, 2D carbon materials are promising due to their functionalized surfaces, which enable stronger hydrogen binding, despite hindrances like aggregation and cost. However, at cryogenic temperatures, their lack of a 3D interconnected structure limits gas diffusion and storage efficiency. Currently, the best hydrogen storage capacity range for carbon-based materials lies between 4.65 and 6.5 wt% obtained experimentally at ambient conditions. However, studies using DFT and Monte Carlo calculations show higher values up to 8 wt%. Creating affordable materials and techniques that possess the necessary kinetics and thermodynamics is a primary obstacle in the field of hydrogen storage technologies. The review highlights some main points: The most prevalently used methods to improve hydrogen storage characteristics are incorporation of different elements/catalysts, nanostructuring and nanoconfinement, and chemical and physical activation of biomass and coal-based carbons. Several studies based on carbon structures, entailing graphene, graphite, nanotube, and fullerene, have been investigated for hydrogen storage, involving DFT studies, and promising results have been acquired. As a result, various approaches, such as defect engineering and surface functionalization, have been applied to enforce the hydrogen storage properties of these structures. These strategies allow us to improve hydrogen storage in carbon structures such as graphene, carbon nanotubes, and fullerenes. Nanostructuring has improved the surface area of carbonaceous materials. It also affects better hydrogen storage capacities due to the formation of nanosized pores. The ultimate objective is to craft carbon-based materials capable of achieving a hydrogen storage capacity of around 6.5 wt% while maintaining the essential adsorption/desorption rate under standard room temperature and pressure conditions. Although some materials have potential storage capacities, difficulties still exist in properly integrating carbon-based materials with hydrogen storage technologies. Therefore, addressing upcoming issues should be a primary focus.
